name: Lansoprazole
summary: Lansoprazole is a proton pump inhibitor, a medicine that lowers stomach acid, used for indigestion, heartburn, reflux disease and stomach ulcers. It is available on prescription only, and longer-term use is reviewed by a doctor because it is linked to low magnesium, vitamin B12 deficiency, bone fractures and gut infections.
usedFor: Reflux disease, where stomach acid flows back up towards the gullet
howItWorks: Lansoprazole belongs to a group of medicines called proton pump inhibitors. It dampens down the enzymes in the lining of the stomach that make acid, so less acid is produced. Having less acid is what eases symptoms such as indigestion, heartburn and reflux.
onset: Symptoms usually start to improve within 2 to 3 days, although the full effect can take up to 4 weeks.

common: Headache, which usually eases after the first week
Feeling sick, diarrhoea, stomach pain and constipation
An itchy or mild rash, dizziness or tiredness, and a dry mouth
Common side effects are usually mild and tend to go away when the medicine is stopped
serious: Worsening stomach pain, yellowing of the skin or whites of the eyes, or dark urine can signal inflammation of the pancreas or liver and needs a same-day call to the GP or NHS 111
Joint pain together with a red rash on sun-exposed skin can signal a skin form of lupus and needs a same-day call to the GP or NHS 111
Severe or persistent diarrhoea can signal an inflamed bowel and needs a same-day call to the GP or NHS 111

A serious allergic reaction (anaphylaxis) is rare; swelling of the lips, mouth, throat or tongue, fast or difficult breathing, a tight throat, trouble swallowing, blue, grey or pale skin, sudden confusion or fainting needs a 999 call

Low blood magnesium is possible after more than 3 months of use and can cause tiredness, dizziness, muscle twitches or an irregular heartbeat, which calls for a GP appointment or NHS 111 if it happens
Use for more than a year may raise the chance of bone fractures, gut infections and vitamin B12 deficiency

cautions: Most adults and children can take lansoprazole, but the NHS advises checking with a doctor first in liver problems, pregnancy, trying for a baby, breastfeeding, low vitamin B12 or before an endoscopy
Lansoprazole may hide some of the problems an endoscopy would usually find
It is not used by people who are allergic to lansoprazole or any ingredient in the product
People with osteoporosis or taking corticosteroids are advised to tell their doctor, because proton pump inhibitors have been linked to fractures of the wrist, hip and spine
Antacids can reduce how much lansoprazole the body takes in, so the pharmacist or doctor advises on timing
St John's wort is best avoided because it may stop lansoprazole working as well as it should
Medicines that can interact include digoxin, itraconazole, ketoconazole, posaconazole, methotrexate, HIV medicines, rifampicin, warfarin, fluvoxamine, tacrolimus and theophylline
It can make the emergency contraceptive ellaOne less effective, while regular contraceptive pills are not affected unless vomiting or severe diarrhoea stops the pill working
Alcohol is not ruled out, but too much increases stomach acid and can make symptoms worse
In pregnancy the NHS says omeprazole is usually offered instead of lansoprazole
While breastfeeding it can be taken, with attention to feeding problems, constipation, diarrhoea, vomiting or unsettled behaviour in the baby, and fertility does not appear to be affected
Dizziness or tiredness can occur, so care is advised before driving or using machinery
monitoring: A doctor regularly reviews whether continued treatment is still needed, particularly with long-term use. Clotting tests may be needed alongside warfarin, and blood levels of tacrolimus may be monitored when lansoprazole is started or stopped.

sections.heading: What is lansoprazole used for?
sections.body:
Lansoprazole is a medicine that lowers the amount of acid made in the stomach. It is prescribed for indigestion, heartburn, reflux disease and stomach ulcers, and occasionally for Zollinger-Ellison syndrome. Reflux disease is the name for stomach acid repeatedly flowing back up into the gullet. In the UK it is only available on prescription. It comes as capsules that are swallowed and as orodispersible tablets that melt in the mouth.

Local prescribing guidance describes the melting tablets as the choice for people who find swallowing difficult.

sections.heading: How does lansoprazole work, and how quickly?
sections.body:
Lansoprazole is a proton pump inhibitor. It dampens down the enzymes in the lining of the stomach that make acid, so less acid is produced. Symptoms usually start to improve within 2 to 3 days. The full effect can take up to 4 weeks.

How long treatment lasts is decided by the prescriber and depends on the reason it was started.

sections.heading: What are the side effects?
sections.body:
The NHS lists headache, feeling sick, diarrhoea, stomach pain, constipation, an itchy or mild rash, dizziness or tiredness, and a dry mouth as common side effects. They are usually mild and tend to go away when the medicine is stopped. Headaches usually ease after the first week.

Serious side effects are rare, affecting fewer than 1 in 1,000 people according to the NHS. Worsening stomach pain, yellowing of the skin or eyes, or dark urine can signal inflammation of the pancreas or liver. Joint pain with a red rash on sun-exposed skin can signal a skin form of lupus. Severe or persistent diarrhoea can signal an inflamed bowel. Any of these needs a same-day call to the GP or NHS 111.

A serious allergic reaction (anaphylaxis) is rare. Swelling of the lips, mouth, throat or tongue, fast or difficult breathing, a tight throat, trouble swallowing, blue, grey or pale skin, sudden confusion or fainting needs a 999 call straight away.

sections.heading: Taking lansoprazole with other medicines, alcohol and contraception
sections.body:
Antacids can reduce how much lansoprazole the body takes in, so a pharmacist or doctor advises on timing. St John's wort is best avoided because it may stop lansoprazole working as well as it should. Medicines that can interact include digoxin, itraconazole, ketoconazole, posaconazole, methotrexate, HIV medicines, rifampicin, warfarin, fluvoxamine, tacrolimus and theophylline. The NHS says there is not enough information to say that other complementary medicines and herbal remedies are fine to take with it.

Alcohol is not ruled out, but too much increases stomach acid and can make symptoms worse. Regular contraceptive pills are not affected, although vomiting or severe diarrhoea can stop a pill working. Lansoprazole can make the emergency contraceptive ellaOne less effective, so another option may be suggested.

sections.heading: Who needs extra care, and what about long-term use?
sections.body:
Most adults and children can take lansoprazole, but the NHS advises checking with a doctor first in liver problems, pregnancy, trying for a baby, breastfeeding, low vitamin B12 or before an endoscopy. Lansoprazole may hide some of the problems an endoscopy would usually find. It is not used by people who are allergic to lansoprazole or any ingredient in the product. People with osteoporosis or taking corticosteroids are advised to tell their doctor.

In pregnancy the NHS says omeprazole is usually offered instead of lansoprazole. While breastfeeding it can be taken, with attention to feeding problems, constipation, diarrhoea, vomiting or unsettled behaviour in the baby.

Taking lansoprazole for more than a year may raise the chance of bone fractures, gut infections and vitamin B12 deficiency. Low blood magnesium is possible after more than 3 months, and can cause tiredness, dizziness, muscle twitches or an irregular heartbeat. For this reason a doctor regularly reviews whether treatment should continue.

faqs.q: How long does lansoprazole take to work?
faqs.a: The NHS says symptoms usually start to improve within 2 to 3 days. The full effect can take up to 4 weeks, so it can take time to judge whether it is helping.

faqs.q: Can I drink alcohol while on lansoprazole?
faqs.a: The NHS does not rule out alcohol. It says too much alcohol increases stomach acid and can make symptoms worse.

faqs.q: Is it all right to take lansoprazole for a long time?
faqs.a: Long-term use is something a doctor keeps under review. The NHS says use for more than a year may raise the chance of bone fractures, gut infections and vitamin B12 deficiency, and low magnesium is possible after more than 3 months. Anyone wondering about stopping after long use can ask the prescriber or pharmacist.

faqs.q: Does lansoprazole affect the contraceptive pill?
faqs.a: The NHS says regular contraceptive pills are not affected. Vomiting or severe diarrhoea can stop a pill working, and lansoprazole can make the emergency contraceptive ellaOne less effective.

faqs.q: Can lansoprazole be taken in pregnancy or while breastfeeding?
faqs.a: In pregnancy the NHS says omeprazole is usually offered instead of lansoprazole. While breastfeeding, it can be taken, with attention to the baby for feeding problems, constipation, diarrhoea, vomiting or unsettled behaviour.
